raw_case_text:
The patient, male, 20 years old, was diagnosed with Hemophilia. At the age of 2 due to continuous bleeding upon trauma. The patient was then treated with multiple infusion of coagulation factor VIII. In 2002, the patient was diagnosed with HIV infection combined with type B hepatitis and type C hepatitis virus infection. CD4+T cell was 70 cell/muL in May 2002 and rose to 200 cell/muL after the treatment using the highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). The right thigh swelling occurred in 2005 and was tentatively diagnosed as hematoma which increased gradually. On June 18, 2007, the patient was admitted to the Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center due to the swollen right thigh. The admission diagnoses were the following: (1) the right thigh hematoma, (2) AIDS, (3) hemophilia, (4) hepatitis C, and (5) hepatitis B. 
A group of surgical experts have been invited to consult on the case after the patient was admitted to the surgical ward. The consultation session concluded that the surgical indication is clear, but with extremely high risk for surgery. The initial treatment plan followed the conservative guideline. However, the hematoma increased gradually with oozing wound which exudated blood and body fluid daily and led to hypoalbuminemia with severe anemia. The patient was put on nutritional support such as albumin and the blood transfusion with daily dose of VIII factor 6000 u that maitin active VIII factor 40%-60%, human serum albumin 1 unit, infusion of the washed red blood cells 2 u every other day, plasma 200 mL in addition to the antivirus, antibiotics, and other drugs which added up to a daily healthcare cost of over 10 K RMB only to merely maintain the basic life-support with hemoglobin in the 15-40 g/L range. The heart failure and kidney failures occurred during the conservative treatment which required symptomatic treatment and intensive care. 
After careful preparation, the patient's CD4 level rose to 272 cell/muL with the hemoglobin of 50.8 g/L and HIV-1 viral load dropped to below the detection level. On July 28, 2009, the joint relief operation was performed in patient's right hip under general anesthesia with intraoperative radial artery and central venous pressure monitoring (Figure 1). 2000 u of factor VIII infusion was applied before the operation followed by 4000 u of VIII factor during the operation. The operating room implemented standard disinfection and isolation procedures to prevent occupational exposure of the healthcare professionals to the HIV during the surgery. After the skin incision was made on the patient's right thigh, the truncated surface was carefully separated to cut off the blood vessels and minimize surgical bleeding. The right hip joint capsule was cut and the femoral neck had crisp fracture with bleeding on the femoral neck cross-section. The femoral head was removed from the acetabulum carefully and the drainage was placed followed by the suture closure of stump. The vital signs remained stable during the operation. The vital signs remained stable during the operation and 3 weeks after amputation, the cross-section wound first degree heal (Figure 2). Patient's overall health condition improved significantly ten months after operation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male with severe hemophilia presenting with a progressively enlarging, ulcerated right thigh mass and chronic bloody fluid exudation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had severe congenital hemophilia and initially developed right thigh swelling in 2005, which was tentatively diagnosed as a hematoma and gradually expanded over two years. By June 2007, the lesion had formed a massive ulcerated mass exuding blood and bodily fluid daily, resulting in profound anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and subsequent heart and renal failure requiring intensive medical resuscitation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe hemophilia A diagnosed at age 2 following persistent post-traumatic bleeding, treated with repeated factor VIII infusions. Chronic retroviral disease co-infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) diagnosed in 2002 (baseline CD4+ T-cell count 70 cells/mcL, rising to 200 cells/mcL on HAART).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right thigh swelling, local pain, daily bloody exudation, fatigue, and dyspnea; negative for fever or acute neurological deficits. Home medications: factor VIII concentrate infusions, antiretroviral therapy. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: General: cachectic, severely pale, with signs of hyperdynamic circulation and congestive heart failure. Right lower extremity: massive swelling of the right thigh with an open, chronic ulcerated wound exuding serosanguinous fluid and blood.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: profound refractory anemia fluctuating between 15 and 40 g/L (1.5-4.0 g/dL), rising to 50.8 g/L (5.08 g/dL) after intensive transfusion therapy; severe hypoalbuminemia; active Factor VIII levels maintained at 40%-60% on replacement therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: Right hip and thigh imaging: massive expansile hematoma / hemophilic pseudotumor involving the right thigh with pathologic fracture of the right femoral neck.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Massive right thigh hemophilic pseudotumor with cutaneous fistulization, severe refractory anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and high-output cardiac and renal decompensation in a patient with severe hemophilia A, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS, chronic hepatitis B, and chronic hepatitis C. Preoperative stabilization achieved CD4 count of 272 cells/mcL and undetectable HIV-1 viral load on antiretroviral therapy. Management & Outcome: Managed preoperatively with daily Factor VIII infusions (6,000 U daily targeting 40%-60% activity), human serum albumin, packed washed red blood cells (2 units every other day), fresh frozen plasma (200 mL), and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Underwent successful right hip joint disarticulation / amputation under general anesthesia with intra-arterial and central venous pressure monitoring, supported by perioperative Factor VIII (2,000 U preoperatively, 4,000 U intraoperatively) and strict infection control precautions. Primary surgical wound healing achieved by 3 weeks postoperatively, with dramatic improvement in systemic health at 10-month follow-up.
